newsitem.title: USA: Apple to release cheaper, faster PCs.
newsitem.headline: Apple to release cheaper, faster PCs.

text.p: Apple Computer Inc. plans to sell lots of cheaper, better-performing personal computers this year and will unveil a new global advertising campaign, the PC maker's chief operating officer said Wednesday.

As part of Apple's three-year plan to turn its fortunes around, the company also will continue to simplify its product lines while introducing powerful laptop and multimedia computers to compete against a new generation of PCs based on Intel Corp. chips, Chief Operating Officer Marco Landi told a news conference at this week's Macworld trade show.
"The mission that we have set up for ourselves is to make sure that we are the leader in providing simple-to-use, powerful, very-high-performance products," Landi said.
Among the products to be introduced will be a $999 Macintosh to rival PCs based on Intel Pentium microprocessors with the same price, he said.

The Cupertino, Calif.-based company also will introduce a high-end Macintosh based on a 533-megahertz PowerPC microprocessor -- a computer chip that the company claims to be one of the fastest widely available.
The company also plans to introduce better-performing PowerBook laptops, traditionally one of Apple's most profitable products.

When Apple hired Gilbert Amelio as chairman and chief executive last February to turn the company around, he set up a plan under which the company would stop its huge financial losses in 1996, introduce new products in 1997 and increase the company's revenues again by 1998.

While Apple did cut costs substantially in 1996, it expects to report a loss of $100 million to $150 million in its fiscal first quarter ended Dec. 27. The company last week blamed weak sales of consumer PCs for the expected loss.

Landi acknowledged that Apple made mistakes in selling to consumers, which account for about 40 percent of its revenues in the Christmas quarter. But Apple is still in good shape to carry out its product plans in 1997, he said.
The $1.7 billion in cash that Apple has on hand is a "strong, solid base for us to make the investments to execute our strategy," he said.
Apple will use some of that cash this month to launch a global advertising campaign aimed at bolstering its image. The campaign will be based on the slogan "Give your dreams a chance," Landi said.
